claims.text: Increasing configurational entropy broadens the alloy's local vibrational spectrum.
Broadening of the local vibrational spectrum enhances electron–phonon coupling.
Enhanced electron–phonon coupling stabilizes an isotropic s-wave superconducting state despite dirty-limit disorder.
The starting alloy is a homogeneous single-phase alloy with a controlled structure such as BCC.
The starting alloy has not demonstrated clear low-temperature superconductivity.
Adding transition metals in near-equiatomic proportions increases configurational entropy.
The chemistry can be modified to increase configurational entropy while retaining the same crystal structure.
Known superconducting high-entropy alloys can enter the superconducting state below 10 K.
Greater chemical complexity produces local lattice distortions and broadened phonon modes.
The disorder-induced structural and vibrational changes adjust the electronic density of states near the Fermi level.
A critical level of chemical randomness makes disorder-induced electron scattering beneficial to superconducting pairing.
The higher-entropy alloy will have a higher superconducting transition temperature than the baseline.
The higher-entropy alloy will exhibit more robust zero resistance, improved critical current density, and greater critical-field robustness than the baseline.
Superconductivity will appear or become stronger as disorder increases up to an optimum.
The proposed disorder mechanism applies to single-phase high-entropy alloys with similar BCC or CsCl-type structures.
Phase separation or a structural transition caused by excessive alloying can invalidate the proposed effect.
Excessively high disorder may increase electron scattering enough to suppress superconductivity.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts enhancement only up to an unspecified optimum and expressly allows excessive disorder to suppress superconductivity or cause the mechanism to cease applying, yet the falsification rule treats suppression by excessive disorder as falsification. That result is therefore simultaneously an allowed boundary behavior and a stated falsifier.
